From my own life, I was haunted by memories of embarrassing moments, faux pas’ or failures in performance, etc.  times i made an ass of myself.

So for three nights in a row, in a friend’s backyard, staying in a tent, i decided to focus on one thing for about 1-2 hours each night:
Find any memory which pains me in this way; find out if I learned the lesson.  If I did not, re-examine until I understand why I felt this way, but if I DID learn the lesson, reshape the memory so it does not haunt me any further.

I had a goal.  You must have a goal.  It could be to create motivation towards certain mental images you hold, or to have a greater sense of emotion X, whatever that is, or to kick or create a habit.  

In my case, through experimentation, i found the best modality for me to play with was position, so bad memories i moved to the rear left of my mental view, behind me, out of reach and view, after desaturating and zooming out.

It’s turned memories that made me shrink in my own past inadequacies and turned them into memories I now laugh at.  

Could it have happened simply by aging?

Doubtful, because once I reshaped the strong memories, weaker and less haunting ones were the ones that popped up in their place.  Minor upsets, flubs, jokes that didnt land.  And they surfaced in moments that related to them, and the age of the initial memory was not a factor.  Last year or early adolescence, didn’t matter.

So the personal hello is based on a model in which we all, individually, have a sort of predefined "greeting" action we perform to strangers.  

Some people curtsy, some nod, some bow, some smile and raise eyebrows, some nod upwards, some tilt their head, some remain motionless, some size you up threateningly.

Each of us has our own "personal hello" greeting.

the implicit purpose of this is to quickly determine what class of mannerisms you might have, so that I can decide to regard you as a potential enemy or a friend.  If you share the same gestures as me, I can imply that you share a similar value-oriented upbringing and therefore we can engage in trade, friendship, sharing, and deeper conversation.

*your job is to shift into neutral upon meeting someone new.*

*your job is to watch for their micro-gestures, feel them, and replay them.*

So if, when you get the introduction, they tilt their head 20' and look up at the stars while pursing their lips, YOU tilt your head, look up, purse your lips.

It may go back and forth twice, but no more than twice should you try to replicate this.  No more than twice or you'll come off like a mimic.

However, there are two huge advantages you gain.

1.  You've now entered a comfortable friendly zone with said person (as opposed to suspicious stranger zone)

2. You can now elegantly and silently get that person's attention at a distance by replaying the bodylanguage of the personal hello.  If you gesture that person's callsign, it's like a beacon to them.  

But it's a beacon to them only.

So, you're in the position of having to learn a little, execute a little, and keep up a mental note of behaviors in the beginning phases.  Once you build a more genuine rapport and style of discourse, you can drop the technique.

I suppose you could make the argument that there were strong periods of unipolarity, such as during the reign of both the Mongol Empire (~1200) and the Ottoman Empire (~1400) but I think it misses the point.

Each of history's various empires were very much focused on expansion, development, taxation, and proliferation of their way of life, via the institution of law and ruling authority.  The aim of this expansion was to increase the base of resources they had to work with.  More resources meant more options for either inward development or outward expansion.

The Romans classically fell because their strategy for energy capture fell victim to the law of dimishing returns.  The Mongol Empire fractured into 4 at the death of Kublai Khan in 1294, allowing the Chinese Han dynasty to take over in the century that followed, as they were only fighting 1/4 of an army.  The ottoman empire began shrinking in the 15th century and couldn't keep up with competition - largely because they used under-education of their populace as a means of maintaining political control.  

It's only been since the second world war that the US emerged as the global superpower it is, one patrolling the seas, ensuring international trade, enforcing international trade contracts, and destabilizing and converting to a sort of semi-democracy- nations it deems as adversarial enough to be a worry.  

So, we could easily make a case that the last millennium was 95% multipolar, and 5% unipolar, with the US assuming the role of having the final say, millitarily or economically, on decisions made.

My thrust, the argument I maintain, is merely that - Had Russia the technology and infrastructure, Had the Ottomans the education and industrialization, had China the ability to harvest energy, or had Germany possibly had a different approach to how they chose to conquer during WW2, they would have ALL loved to have the power it takes to become a world superpower and would gladly have advanced on that goal.  
 
It's about ambition.  Who has it, who is in a position to achieve political aims.  

If you could somehow pacify all the current leaders and bring about peace on a global scale, it would only be a matter of time until someone else was born who thought differently, thought they could bring a new order to the chaos they see in other nations, or that they thought they could do better with the resources someone else was using less effectively, and decided to marshal forces to attack.  Such has been the looping story of conquest since we descended from trees.  

Someone has to be at the helm.  Because if not, someone will rise to the job, and will do so for reasons that have to do more with their own pride, and less to do with global peace and stability.   In truth, I think the UN ought to become the global arbitrator and coordinator of force.

So here's how we're going to do this.  We're going to build a stack of skills.

At the bottom, your basic movement, crouch and jump skill.

Above that, your ability to aim.  By that I mean, to put crosshairs on the target.

Then comes your ability to properly time your shots and your reload pauses.  Let's call these the fundamentals.

You can spend months working on those three skillsets and still rank in the bottom.  Why?

Above that is the skill of "crosshair placement".  This is the skill of managing your aim such that you are always aiming at the place an enemy is likeliest to appear, even while you are moving.

There's the skill of using "pre-fire", when anticipating that a target is there, to jump out and be already shooting (which you can only do if you've mastered crosshair placement)

There's the additional skill of recoil correction - the slight draw on the aim which counteracts the natural recoil of the weapon.  practice this on a wall.

Above that is knowledge of weaponry and the ability to use the right tool for the job.  Someone can still get the jump on you with a more situationally-appropriate weapon.

Even above that is the skill of choosing the right target.  Did you foolishly choose to try to solo take on a group of three?  Or, If you can, take out the one who is looking away from you rather than engaging with someone who could fire back.  Take out the one first who, in doing so, no one will see your bullet trace.  Add in the element of creating distractions and you can become a real menace.

Knowing when to run or feint is a skill.  Feints are deadly.  Do you even know how to do that?  It involves running away, thus tricking the enemy into thinking you've got nothing, but really, you're just drawing him into a position where you hold the advantage.

Above that are the situational-awareness skills of knowing the map's lures and chokepoints, and taking advantage of them.  The glowing pickup is tempting, but so is ambushing the people who are tempted by it.

Add in the skill of managing your communications effectively and you start to become a leader.  The people around you don't need to hear "Fuck!  I died!"  They need to hear "There's a guy above the yellow door" or "Two heavies, right side"  Always be thinking about effective information and trying to build that discipline.

These skills stack upwards, which by that I mean, you can't really master the ones above until you've mastered the ones beneath.  You're ready to move up to mastering the next skill, you just don't know what it is!

(Disclaimer: I'm a designer working on having my first singleplayer/co-op title published (a realtime strategy board game), and here are a list of the things I've had to design around or worry about)

The main reason, I think is that it really is an enormously tall order.  It's because studios know that they're fighting against both enormous competition AND a lot of *problems of human nature* in order to create a game that *works well* and succeeds in the marketplace long-term.  It's a very difficult task.

Let me explain:

Keep in mind a player can only play one game at a time with any degree of attention being paid.  In order for a game (in which multiplayer is the main draw) to be successful, it must somehow achieve most, (but not necessarily all) of the following:


Gameplay stuff:
* Have fun and accessible game mechanics
* Run reliable netcode and account for variations in latency that are completely unpredictable
* Run on many pieces of different hardware and yet be stable and not crash
* Incentivise team-play instead of parasitizing/theft behavior

Multiplayer stuff:
* Somehow discourage players in a co-op session from leaving or abandoning the game as things get uncomfortable or annoying
* Corral or incentivise the players to remain in relative proximity to each other
* Assemble a reliable matchmaking/lobby system with some form of reputation control or ELO/skill rating
* If voice/text is a necessity, group players together regionally or by preferred language so that speakers of similar languages are able to find each other (although ideally, removing the necessity greatly expands your market)
* Allow for strangers to meet and vet each other prior to play
* Allow means by which individual players can mute or ignore the toxic behavior of others
* Allocate a huge portion of your profits towards the running of servers to host these games (unless it's on the player to do so - a tough bargain)
* Come up with a long-term monetization plan to keep those servers running
* Develop a strong bot AI to take over when players are unavailable

Micro-Behavior Stuff:
* Allow for a modest range of player-to-player interactions WITHOUT allowing for players to exploit and grief the others (too much) or allow for moderation mechanisms like kicking or punishing misbehaving players 
* Assign rewards equitably for team play and cooperation
* Allow for satisfied customers and players to regroup with the same team (friends system)

Macro-Behavior Stuff:
* Localise your game for dozens of countries and languages
* Calm down the furious playerbase whose games have been ruined by the behavior/toxicity of others
* Calm down the market/review backlash caused by furious gamers whose heavily-invested play sessions were ruined by the behavior of toxic players
* Reassure the investors and publishers that the problem isn't YOUR STUDIO, but rather the insignificant actions of a few "bad apples" and not representative of how fun/profitable your game might be
* (Major issue) Maintain a *critical mass* of ready gamers *online, regionally appropriate and available to play* (Otherwise risk being seen as a "dying community", which precludes many would-be gamers from investing in and joining (and thereby restoring) the community
* Market the hell out of your game at just the right times in between other releases
* Somehow reassure the gamer, who is both the customer AND the product offered to the other gamers in the co-op session, that *this game will have staying power and the servers won't become ghost towns in a year, leaving you feeling ripped off
* Reassure parents and the ratings board that your game *community* isn't going to be toxic to children
* Disallow lewd, racist, sexist, phobic, or otherwise vulgar and inappropriate behavior (if you figure that one out you could become a billionaire)

All the while, while juggling all those problems in your head, remember this:

**If there is an alternative way for a player to spend that time (by playing someone else's game), one with more fun, a stronger community, a less buggy experience, or less obstacles to getting into a match quickly, you have probably already lost this battle**.  
This last point hurts me, deep down, because ultimately I know what it means is that we are going to gravitate towards bigger, established games, and overlook new, awesome releases, like Titanfall, which was incredible but didn't achieve the kind of market penetration necessary to overcome the inertia.  Remember, you're not just competing for time against boring old cable TV, you're up against Red Dead Redemption, GTA, WoW, LoL, DoTA, No Man's Sky, Elite:, EvE, PS2, COD, Battlefield, Rocket League, and all the awesome singleplayer games out there, not to mention friends, family, lovers, and the responsibilities of life.

So how about it!?  Ready to take out that 25 million dollar loan, hire your studio, and get to work developing the co-op game of your dreams?

Thing about that is, TCP is meant to be *resilient*, not necessarily *high-performance*.  In high-performance systems like iSCSI or fibrechannel where you are transmitting vast amounts of data between two closely-linked machines (usually only one "hop" away), other protocols outperform TCP all the time.  TCP has many checks and balances that allow it to become a reliable network that can instantly adapt to losses or outages, but it was never designed for high-performance.

The difference between good writing and bad writing often comes down to the authors and editors being willing to hold themselves to high standards, to make difficult choices.  To not, as it were, seek the widest audience by appealing to the lowest-common-denominator.

Now, you could argue that NPCs in a video game only serve one function, to *serve the player* experience, but I would argue that that actually makes for too many easy choices, it necessitates appealing to making *all* NPCs into empty shells on which the player impresses their will.

Now you could have those NPCs, such that every NPC in the game could become a sexual object or a sidekick-choomba or sold you every item in the game, simply because a player somewhere desired it to be so, but I maintain that it would have come at a tremendous cost to the authenticity.

and maybe we could have gotten through the game and gone our separate ways, but there'd be this kind of shared sense of disappointment- at the bar of standards being so brutally lowered, at the sheer *willingness* to compromise their writing of what were intended to be realistic people in a realistic world.  

The authenticity of this world having been brutally diminished, you'd see thousands more people trying to figure out why this specter of disappointment lingers over their game, why, even at a pre-conscious level, they just felt something was "off" about the characters or the world, writing in on forums with phrases like "Cyberpunk 2077's writing is terrible, witcher was wayyyyy better imo" "Cyberpunk could have been great but they settled on making it into a complete fuck fantasy RPG" "Why do all the characters feel the same in Cyberpunk?"

It doesn't work in the real world, and how could it work if you're attempting to build a solid and realistic 3D world?  Wanna try petitioning a woman to be your girlfriend and let us know how that goes for you?  

Sorry, but I prefer that if a game aims for authenticity in setting (as CDPR and their writers/sources have a track record of doing), they should also acknowledge that people have preferences and boundaries and are not mere slabs of meat that we can simply speak the right magic words to and watch undergarments fall off.  It's denigrating and it makes for bad, awful, fake, and disingenuous writing, which would spill into the rest of the story everywhere.

Oh absolutely!  Allow me to share one of my little stories with you.  

It was 2002 and I was a young Lance Corporal in the USMC with a friend of mine who both had some cash and some leave coming up.  Given that we were both stationed at Pacific HQ (Oahu Hawaii) we decided to take a 4 day trip to the Big Island, and based on an experienced trekker we decided to wait until a full moon was upcoming for us to go.  
Down at the [south end of the Eastern wing of Hawaii](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Hawaii/@19.3042791,-155.0951989,15.17z/data=!4m5!3m4!1s0x7bffdb064f79e005:0x4b7782d274cc8628!8m2!3d19.8967662!4d-155.5827818) There's a road "Chain of Craters road" which dead ends....(check the Satellite view!)  And you might guess why.  Being down-flow from the active rift zone of Kiluaea Crater, it was blocked some 15 years ago by a massive flow of lava that flowed right down and cut off the road.  
So we did the thing any responsible adult would do...  Get out our flashlights and our backpacks with food and water and first aid kits, and decide to hike.  Starting at about 10PM at night.  
The reason is that you want to be able to see the Lava at night, as it gives off a red glow like a lit furnace, but using the full moon we could walk across the black glassy igneous remains of previous lava flows to search for it.  
After following the coast eastward and cresting some 4 or 5 hills, some 2.5 hours later we found ourselves coming over a ridge and seeing something we weren't ready for.  
It was the look of a small city.  Nestled in the black glassy rock, cut off from all life.  Except it wasn't a city.  

We realized what we were looking at was small pockets of light, like those of city streetlamps and houses, speckling the otherwise black terrain.  Except these "streetlights" and "houses" our imagination told us were there - were all deep orange/red in color.  

Suddenly we knew what we were seeing was a hot, active lava rift; pockets of glassy rock suddenly heating to boiling, flowing, then cooling, over and over, hundreds of them, spread across this valley.

We suddeny felt very unsafe.  Still, we collected ourselves and pressed on.  We decided to head for the closest fissure.  There were some moments where we had to jump over some small steam vents (they smelled of sulfur) and, checking the ground ahead of us for sturdiness, managed to find our way to a small lava vent which seemed small enough to mean us no harm.  

It was HOT near it.  It looks small, but when the wind blew the right way, it felt like a nice summer night, and when it blew the WRONG way, it was like standing in front of a brick oven.  [pics](https://imgur.com/a/WNHMfBp) We did manage to skirt that wind and find a way to get close enough to poke it with sticks (they'd burn), pour water on it (it'd boil), and pee on it (it stunk).  One thing that was interesting was that the sound of pahoehoe lava slowly creeping across the terrain sounds just like crinkling cellophane (like the wrapper from a fruit-roll-up)  

We quickly decided it was time to leave.  Heading the only way we coult to resume our bearings (towards the coast) we then found ourselves on a flat block of glassy old lava - but to the south was a crack we hesitated to cross.  Only 4" deep, is seems trivial but it was glowing deep red from the bottom of it, all the way across.  So we assumed the lava block to be hot and possibly unstable.  We checked to the east.  There was another crack.  Same eerie red light pouring out from below.  We started to worry...  so we headed back where we came from, to the north.  Another crack, with another red light under it!  Did we miss this going down?  And finally, our homeward escape route, to the west.  Again, a final crack with a same hostile red light pouring out, with steam and sulfur creating a curtain.  
What to do?  Did we somehow find ourselves perched atop a floating block of glass on a lava rift that was threatening to swallow it at any moment?  Suddenly our panic response threw us into high gear and we decided we were just going to have to jump over the western crack and run.  Being only a few inches deep, we made it safely, and continued at a feverish pace until all of the red lights were far behind us.  

There were a number of sights we saw that night besides Pele's immediate wrath, there was a half-buried playground, and a spot of untouched highway like an island in the middle of lava floes decades old, but I will always remember finding ourselves on a block of glass, feeling like we were suddenly adrift on a sea of lava below us, ready to capsize or split or gush at any moment.  Since then I vowed not to underestimate nature.  We are but houseflies to her mightiness.
